items.title: Solving an Exponential Growth Problem

key_prerequisites.name: Solving First-Order IVPs Using Separation of Variables

sections.normalized_html:
Suppose that the population [MATH: P(t)] of a town after [MATH: t] years can be modeled by the differential equation

[MATH: \dfrac {\textrm{d}P} {\textrm{d}t} = 0.02P.]

If there are currently [MATH: 500] people in the town, what will be the town's population in [MATH: 3] years?
sections.readable_text:
Suppose that the population [MATH: P(t)] of a town after [MATH: t] years can be modeled by the differential equation

[MATH: \dfrac {\textrm{d}P} {\textrm{d}t} = 0.02P.]

If there are currently [MATH: 500] people in the town, what will be the town's population in [MATH: 3] years?

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
We note that this is an exponential growth differential equation with [MATH: r = 0.02]. Therefore, the solution to this equation is [MATH: P(t) = P_0\,e^{0.02t},] where [MATH: P_0] is the initial value.

We're told that the population is currently [MATH: 500,] so we have [MATH: P_0 = 500.]

Therefore, the population of the town at time [MATH: t] is [MATH: P(t) = 500\,e^{0.02t}.]

Finally, to find the population after [MATH: 3] years, we substitute [MATH: t=3] into the above, as follows:

[MATH: P(3)|= 500e^{0.02 ⋅ 3}; = 500e^{0.06}; ≈ 531]

Therefore, we conclude that the population will be approximately [MATH: 531] after [MATH: 3] years.

sections.normalized_html:
Suppose that the value [MATH: V(t)] of a particular car can be modeled by the differential equation

[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm d V}{\textrm d t} = -0.1V,]

where [MATH: t] is the time, in years, since the car was first purchased. If the car was purchased for [MATH: \[math]10\,000,] what will it be worth after [MATH: 3] years?
sections.readable_text:
Suppose that the value [MATH: V(t)] of a particular car can be modeled by the differential equation

[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm d V}{\textrm d t} = -0.1V,]

where [MATH: t] is the time, in years, since the car was first purchased. If the car was purchased for [MATH: \[math]10\,000,] what will it be worth after [MATH: 3] years?

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, notice that the right-hand side of the equation is negative, which means that the car's value is decreasing.

This is an exponential decay differential equation with [MATH: r = 0.1.] Therefore, the general solution to this equation is

[MATH: V(t) = V_0 e^{-0.1 t}.]

We know that the car was first purchased for [MATH: \[math]10\,000.] Therefore, [MATH: V_0 = 10\,000,] and we have the particular solution

[MATH: V(t) = 10\,000 e^{-0.1 t}.]

To find the car's value after [MATH: 3] years, we substitute [MATH: t=3] into the particular solution above. This gives

[MATH: V(3)|= 10000e^{− 0.1 ⋅ 3}; = 10000e^{− 0.3}; ≈ 7408.]

Therefore, the car will be worth approximately [MATH: \[/math]7\,408] after three years.

items.title: Computing an Unknown Rate

key_prerequisites.name: Solving Equations Containing the Exponential Function

sections.normalized_html: The number of followers of a celebrity's social media account increases at a rate that is directly proportional to the number of followers at that time. Given that there are currently [MATH: 600\,000] followers and in [MATH: 3] months there will be [MATH: 780\,000] followers, what is the growth rate? Round your answer to the nearest percent.
sections.readable_text: The number of followers of a celebrity's social media account increases at a rate that is directly proportional to the number of followers at that time. Given that there are currently [MATH: 600\,000] followers and in [MATH: 3] months there will be [MATH: 780\,000] followers, what is the growth rate? Round your answer to the nearest percent.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The rate [MATH: N'(t)] at which the number of followers increases is directly proportional to the number of followers [MATH: N.] Therefore, we can model the number of followers using the differential equation [MATH: \frac{\mathrm{d} N}{\mathrm{d} t} = rN,] where [MATH: t] is measured in months, and [MATH: r > 0] is the growth rate.

The solution to this equation is [MATH: N(t) = N_0\,e^{rt},] where [MATH: N_0] is the initial number of followers.

We're told that there are currently [MATH: 600\,000] followers, so we have [MATH: N_0 = 600\,000.]

Therefore, the number of followers [MATH: N] after [MATH: t] months is [MATH: N(t) = 600\,000 \, e^{rt} .]

Finally, to find the growth rate, we substitute [MATH: N(3)=780\,000] into the equation above and solve for [MATH: r,] as follows: [MATH: N(3)|= 600000e^{r ⋅ 3}; 780000|= 600000e^{3r}; e^{3r}|= (780000)/(600000); e^{3r}|= 1.3; \ln (e^{3r})|= \ln (1.3); 3r|= \ln (1.3); r|= (1)/(3)\ln (1.3); r|≈ 0.08754]

Therefore, [MATH: r\approx 9\%,] rounded to the nearest percent.

Content:
We have been using the fact that the general solution to the differential equation

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{\mathrm d P}{\mathrm d t} = \pm rP]

Content:
is given by the formula

Content:
[MATH: P(t) = P_0 e^{\pm r t},]

Content:
where [MATH: P_0 = P(0)] is the value of [MATH: P] when [MATH: t=0.] Let's now derive this general solution.

Content:
Our differential equation is separable, so we can solve it by separating variables and then integrating both sides with respect to [MATH: t,] as follows:

Content:
[MATH: (dP)/(dt)|= ± rP; (1)/(P)(dP)/(dt)|= ± r; ∫(1)/(P)(dP)/(dt)dt|= ∫ ± rdt; ∫(1)/(P)dP|= ∫ ± rdt; \ln|P||= ± rt + C;|P||= e^{± rt + C};|P||= e^{C}e^{± rt}; P(t)|= ± e^{C}e^{± rt}; P(t)|= Ke^{± rt},]

Content:
where [MATH: K=\pm e^C] is a constant. Substituting [MATH: t=0,] we get
[MATH: P(0)|= Ke^{0} = K,]

Content:
and our model becomes
[MATH: P(t) = P(0) e^{\pm rt}.]

Content:
Lastly, it is common to denote [MATH: P(0)] by [MATH: P_0.] Doing this, we have
[MATH: P(t) = P_0 e^{\pm rt}.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
We often model real-life situations using a differential equation of the form
[MATH: \dfrac{\mathrm dP}{\mathrm dt} = rP,]
where [MATH: P = P(t),] and [MATH: r>0] is a constant of proportionality.

Content:
This differential equation is used to model a quantity [MATH: P] whose value increases at a rate that is proportional to the quantity [MATH: P] itself.

Content:
The general solution of this differential equation is given by

Content:
[MATH: P(t) = P_0 e^{r t},]

Content:
where [MATH: P_0 = P(0).] We will derive this general solution at the end of this lesson.

Content:
A typical solution curve is shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/012d5736fc7012d675521bfe1e58b101]

Content:
Notice that [MATH: P(t)] is simply an exponential growth curve. For this reason, the original differential equation is sometimes called an exponential growth differential equation or exponential growth model.

---

Item 2 — Example: Solving an Exponential Growth Problem

Example Prompt:
Suppose that the population [MATH: P(t)] of a town after [MATH: t] years can be modeled by the differential equation

[MATH: \dfrac {\textrm{d}P} {\textrm{d}t} = 0.02P.]

If there are currently [MATH: 500] people in the town, what will be the town's population in [MATH: 3] years?

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We note that this is an exponential growth differential equation with [MATH: r = 0.02]. Therefore, the solution to this equation is
[MATH: P(t) = P_0\,e^{0.02t},]
where [MATH: P_0] is the initial value.

We're told that the population is currently [MATH: 500,] so we have [MATH: P_0 = 500.]

Therefore, the population of the town at time [MATH: t] is
[MATH: P(t) = 500\,e^{0.02t}.]

Finally, to find the population after [MATH: 3] years, we substitute [MATH: t=3] into the above, as follows:

[MATH: P(3)|= 500e^{0.02 ⋅ 3}; = 500e^{0.06}; ≈ 531]

Therefore, we conclude that the population will be approximately [MATH: 531] after [MATH: 3] years.

---

Item 5 — Tutorial: The Exponential Decay Problem

Content:
Now let's consider a differential equation of the form
[MATH: \dfrac{\mathrm dP}{\mathrm dt} = -rP,]
where [MATH: P = P(t),] and [MATH: r>0] is a constant of proportionality.

Content:
This differential equation is used to model a quantity [MATH: P] whose value decreases at a rate that is proportional to the quantity [MATH: P] itself.

Content:
The general solution of this differential equation is given by

Content:
[MATH: P(t) = P_0 e^{-r t},]

Content:
where [MATH: P_0 = P(0).] We will derive this general solution at the end of this lesson.

Content:
A typical solution curve is shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/22bc2fe51a8c9279888e4b4850a0f25b]

Content:
Notice that [MATH: P(t)] is simply an exponential decay curve. For this reason, the original differential equation is sometimes called an exponential decay differential equation or exponential decay model.

---

Item 6 — Example: Solving an Exponential Decay Problem

Example Prompt:
Suppose that the value [MATH: V(t)] of a particular car can be modeled by the differential equation

[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm d V}{\textrm d t} = -0.1V,]

where [MATH: t] is the time, in years, since the car was first purchased. If the car was purchased for [MATH: \[math]10\,000,] what will it be worth after [MATH: 3] years?

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, notice that the right-hand side of the equation is negative, which means that the car's value is decreasing.

This is an exponential decay differential equation with [MATH: r = 0.1.] Therefore, the general solution to this equation is

[MATH: V(t) = V_0 e^{-0.1 t}.]

We know that the car was first purchased for [MATH: \[math]10\,000.] Therefore, [MATH: V_0 = 10\,000,] and we have the particular solution

[MATH: V(t) = 10\,000 e^{-0.1 t}.]

To find the car's value after [MATH: 3] years, we substitute [MATH: t=3] into the particular solution above. This gives

[MATH: V(3)|= 10000e^{− 0.1 ⋅ 3}; = 10000e^{− 0.3}; ≈ 7408.]

Therefore, the car will be worth approximately [MATH: \[/math]7\,408] after three years.

Item 9 — Example: Computing an Unknown Rate

Example Prompt:
The number of followers of a celebrity's social media account increases at a rate that is directly proportional to the number of followers at that time. Given that there are currently [MATH: 600\,000] followers and in [MATH: 3] months there will be [MATH: 780\,000] followers, what is the growth rate? Round your answer to the nearest percent.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The rate [MATH: N'(t)] at which the number of followers increases is directly proportional to the number of followers [MATH: N.] Therefore, we can model the number of followers using the differential equation
[MATH: \frac{\mathrm{d} N}{\mathrm{d} t} = rN,]
where [MATH: t] is measured in months, and [MATH: r > 0] is the growth rate.

The solution to this equation is
[MATH: N(t) = N_0\,e^{rt},]
where [MATH: N_0] is the initial number of followers.

We're told that there are currently [MATH: 600\,000] followers, so we have [MATH: N_0 = 600\,000.]

Therefore, the number of followers [MATH: N] after [MATH: t] months is
[MATH: N(t) = 600\,000 \, e^{rt} .]

Finally, to find the growth rate, we substitute [MATH: N(3)=780\,000] into the equation above and solve for [MATH: r,] as follows:
[MATH: N(3)|= 600000e^{r ⋅ 3}; 780000|= 600000e^{3r}; e^{3r}|= (780000)/(600000); e^{3r}|= 1.3; \ln (e^{3r})|= \ln (1.3); 3r|= \ln (1.3); r|= (1)/(3)\ln (1.3); r|≈ 0.08754]

Therefore, [MATH: r\approx 9\%,] rounded to the nearest percent.

Item 12 — Tutorial: Deriving the General Solution

Content:
We have been using the fact that the general solution to the differential equation

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{\mathrm d P}{\mathrm d t} = \pm rP]

Content:
is given by the formula

Content:
[MATH: P(t) = P_0 e^{\pm r t},]

Content:
where [MATH: P_0 = P(0)] is the value of [MATH: P] when [MATH: t=0.] Let's now derive this general solution.

Content:
Our differential equation is separable, so we can solve it by separating variables and then integrating both sides with respect to [MATH: t,] as follows:

Content:
[MATH: (dP)/(dt)|= ± rP; (1)/(P)(dP)/(dt)|= ± r; ∫(1)/(P)(dP)/(dt)dt|= ∫ ± rdt; ∫(1)/(P)dP|= ∫ ± rdt; \ln|P||= ± rt + C;|P||= e^{± rt + C};|P||= e^{C}e^{± rt}; P(t)|= ± e^{C}e^{± rt}; P(t)|= Ke^{± rt},]

Content:
where [MATH: K=\pm e^C] is a constant. Substituting [MATH: t=0,] we get
[MATH: P(0)|= Ke^{0} = K,]

Content:
and our model becomes
[MATH: P(t) = P(0) e^{\pm rt}.]

Content:
Lastly, it is common to denote [MATH: P(0)] by [MATH: P_0.] Doing this, we have
[MATH: P(t) = P_0 e^{\pm rt}.]
